---
title: Kernel Mixture Densities
---

This page is the technical description of [[numcosmo-math|NcmStatsDist]] and its two
subclasses, [[numcosmo-math|NcmStatsDistKDE]] and [[numcosmo-math|NcmStatsDistVKDE]].
These reconstruct a probability density from a set of sample points and draw from the
result. Their main use in the library is as the proposal of the APES sampler,
[[numcosmo-math|NcmFitESMCMCWalkerAPES]], where the quality of the reconstruction sets
the acceptance of the chain.

## The interpolant

For a $d$-dimensional function $g(x)$, the interpolant is

$$
s(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i \phi\left(|x-x_i|, \Sigma_i\right),
\qquad x \in \mathbf{R}^d,
$$ {#eq-interpolant}

where $x_i$ are the sample points, $\Sigma_i$ sets the scale and shape of the kernel at
$x_i$, and $\lambda_i$ is its weight. The weights are chosen so that

$$
s(x_i) = g(x_i).
$$ {#eq-interp-conditions}

Evaluating the kernels at the sample points gives the interpolation matrix $\Phi$, and
the target values $g(x_i)$ give $G$, so that @eq-interp-conditions reads

$$
G = \lambda \Phi.
$$ {#eq-nnls}

This is solved as a non-negative linear least-squares problem [@LawsonHanson1974], which
keeps $\lambda_i \geq 0$. The weights are then divided by their sum, making them a
probability distribution over the kernels. Sampling draws a kernel with probability
$\lambda_i$, then a point from that kernel. (An earlier version mixed the weights with
the uniform $1/n$ in a fixed proportion; the mixing had no measurable effect on the
sampler at any ensemble size and was removed.) For an introduction to radial basis interpolation see [@DuToit2008].

The caller supplies the target as $-2\ln g(x_i)$, which is the natural form when $g$ is
a posterior.

## The local scale matrices

[[numcosmo-math|NcmStatsDistKDE]] gives every kernel the same $\Sigma_i$: the sample
covariance $C$, a fixed matrix, or a robust estimate. [[numcosmo-math|NcmStatsDistVKDE]]
gives kernel $i$ its own $\Sigma_i$, the covariance of the $k$ sample points nearest to
$x_i$, the neighbors being found in the coordinates whitened by $C$. The number $k$ is
either a fraction of the sample (`local-frac`) or a count per dimension
(`points-per-dim`, $k = \min(n, \lceil c\, d \rceil)$); when $k$ reaches $n$ every
kernel has the covariance $C$ and the estimator is the KDE.

The covariance is taken about the neighbors' own mean $\bar{x}_k$, not about the kernel
center $x_i$. The alternative, the second moment $\frac{1}{k}\sum_j (x_j - x_i)(x_j -
x_i)^T = \frac{k-1}{k} C_k + (\bar{x}_k - x_i)(\bar{x}_k - x_i)^T$, is the maximum
likelihood Gaussian with its center fixed at $x_i$ and looks like the more natural choice
for a kernel centered there. It was implemented and measured, and it is worse at every
neighborhood size: on the out-of-sample acceptance of the resulting proposal (Gaussian, banana,
bimodal, funnel and Rosenbrock targets in 2 to 21 dimensions, 100 walkers per dimension,
$k/n$ from 0.05 to 0.8) it loses between 10 % and a factor of 3, and on a 10-dimensional
funnel at $k/n = 0.05$ it drops the acceptance from 0.23 to 0.001. The reason is the
center shrinkage of the next section: the rank-one term is large for the kernels at the
edge of the sample, so it inflates the mean kernel covariance $\langle\Sigma\rangle$ in
@eq-matrix-budget, every center is then contracted harder, and the interior kernels,
which the term barely changes, end up too narrow for their spacing. Without shrinkage
the two choices agree within noise, so nothing is gained either way. The option was
removed; this paragraph records the choice so that it is not reopened without new
evidence.

## Center shrinkage

A kernel mixture built on the sample points is wider than the sample it came from. The
correction implemented here is the one introduced by @West1993 for mixture
approximations to posteriors, and used since in sequential Monte Carlo.

Sampling the mixture is a two-step draw: select a kernel $I$ with probability
$\lambda_I$, then draw a point from it. Write $\langle \cdot \rangle$ for the average
over that selection, and let $m_I$ and $S_I$ be the center and the covariance of the
selected kernel. The law of total covariance splits the covariance of the result $Y$
into the covariance of the centers and the mean covariance within a kernel,

$$
\mathrm{Cov}(Y) = \mathrm{Cov}\left(m_I\right) + \left\langle S_I \right\rangle.
$$ {#eq-total-cov}

Let $\mu$ and $C$ be the mean and the covariance of the sample points. In an ordinary
kernel density estimate the kernels sit on the sample points and each has covariance
$h^2 C$, with $h$ the bandwidth, so a draw is $Y = x_I + \varepsilon$ with
$\mathrm{Cov}(\varepsilon) = h^2 C$. The first term of @eq-total-cov is $C$ and the
second $h^2 C$,

$$
\mathrm{Cov}(Y) = C + h^2 C = \left(1 + h^2\right) C,
$$ {#eq-kde-inflation}

so the mixture is wider than the sample it is built from, by a factor that grows with
the bandwidth.

Center shrinkage removes that excess by moving the centers toward $\mu$. Placing them at

$$
c_i = \mu + a \left(x_i - \mu\right), \qquad a > 0,
$$ {#eq-centers}

gives them covariance $a^2 C$. Writing the kernel covariance as $b^2 C$, the two terms
of @eq-total-cov are $a^2 C$ and $b^2 C$, so the mixture reproduces $C$ when

$$
a^2 + b^2 = 1.
$$ {#eq-budget}

The centers and the kernels share one covariance budget, and $a$ trades the two against
each other while their sum stays fixed. @West1993 takes $b = h$ directly, so that
$a = \sqrt{1 - h^2}$ and the bandwidth is restricted to $h < 1$. The implementation here
instead narrows the kernels by the same factor it moves the centers, $b = a h$, which
determines both and leaves $h$ unrestricted,

$$
a = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + h^2}}, \qquad b = \frac{h}{\sqrt{1 + h^2}}.
$$ {#eq-a-and-b}

For $h \to 0$, $a \to 1$ and $b \to 0$: the centers stay on the sample points and this
is the narrow-kernel limit of the usual estimate. For $h \to \infty$, $a \to 0$ and
$b \to 1$: the centers collapse onto $\mu$ and each kernel carries the whole of $C$, so
the mixture becomes a single kernel centered at $\mu$ with covariance $C$.

### When the budget is exact

$\mu$ and $C$ are the mean and the covariance of the $n$ sample points that carry the
kernels, both unweighted: $\mu$ is their arithmetic mean and $C$ their unbiased sample
covariance, normalized by $n - 1$. With equal weights the covariance of the centers,
normalized by $n$, is then $r a^2 C$ with $r = (n - 1)/n$, and the implementation
includes that factor, $a^2 r + b^2 = 1$ (@eq-matrix-budget below). The budget therefore
holds exactly when the weights $\lambda_i$ are equal, which is the mixture prepared
without interpolation, the default. As $h \to 0$, $a \to \sqrt{n/(n - 1)}$, slightly
above one: the centers alone then carry $C$. With unequal weights both terms of
@eq-total-cov are $\lambda$-weighted while $\mu$ and $C$ are not, and the budget is
approximate. The weights that come out of @eq-nnls are not equal.

### The general transform

A fixed-bandwidth estimator with the sample covariance gives every kernel the scale
matrix $C$, and a scalar $a$ as in @eq-a-and-b suffices. In general the kernel scale
matrices $\Sigma_i$ are not proportional to $C$ (a fixed or robust covariance in
[[numcosmo-math|NcmStatsDistKDE]], or the per-kernel $\Sigma_i$ of
[[numcosmo-math|NcmStatsDistVKDE]]), and no scalar satisfies @eq-budget as a matrix
equation. The implementation contracts by a matrix instead. With

$$
c_i = \mu + A \left(x_i - \mu\right), \qquad
\Sigma_i \to \hat A \Sigma_i \hat A^T, \qquad
A = a \hat A, \quad \det \hat A = 1,
$$ {#eq-matrix-transform}

and the bandwidth in use $a h$, the two terms of @eq-total-cov are $r A C A^T$ and
$\kappa h^2 A \langle\Sigma\rangle A^T$, where $\langle\Sigma\rangle$ is the mean of
the kernel scale matrices and $\kappa$ the kernel variance factor of the next section, so
the budget reads

$$
A \left(r C + \kappa h^2 \langle\Sigma\rangle\right) A^T = C, \qquad r = \frac{n - 1}{n}.
$$ {#eq-matrix-budget}

With $C = L L^T$ and the eigendecomposition
$L^{-1} \langle\Sigma\rangle L^{-T} = V \mathrm{diag}(s) V^T$, a solution is

$$
A = L V \mathrm{diag}\left[\left(r + \kappa h^2 s_p\right)^{-1/2}\right] V^T L^{-1},
\qquad a = \det(A)^{1/d} = \prod_{p=1}^d \left(r + \kappa h^2 s_p\right)^{-1/(2d)}.
$$ {#eq-matrix-solution}

$L$, $V$ and $s$ depend only on the sample, so they are computed once per preparation;
a new bandwidth only changes the $d$ diagonal entries. Since $s_p \geq 0$ the diagonal is
never singular, and $A$ does not depend on the choice of the factor $L$ (the Cholesky
construction $A = U_C^T U_M^{-T}$, with $M = r C + \kappa h^2 \langle\Sigma\rangle$,
also solves @eq-matrix-budget but changes with the order of the parameters). $\hat A$
has unit determinant, so it leaves every kernel normalization unchanged. For $\langle\Sigma\rangle \propto C$ the transform
is isotropic, $A = a I$ with $a = (r + \kappa h^2)^{-1/2}$, which is @eq-a-and-b up to
$r$; the library detects that case and applies the scalar.

### The kernel variance factor

The covariance of a kernel need not equal the scale matrix it is parameterized by. Their
ratio $\kappa$ is $1$ for [[numcosmo-math|NcmStatsDistKernelGauss]] and $\nu/(\nu-2)$
for [[numcosmo-math|NcmStatsDistKernelST]] with $\nu$ degrees of freedom; it is the
factor in front of $h^2$ in @eq-matrix-budget. Center shrinkage needs a kernel with a
finite covariance, since $\kappa$ has to exist. The Student-t kernel with $\nu \leq 2$,
the Cauchy kernel included, has none and is refused. The sample points $x_i$ remain the
points at which the conditions @eq-interp-conditions are imposed; only the kernels move
and change shape.

## Automatic kernel selection

The bandwidth can be fitted by cross-validation, by one of four objectives: the
out-of-sample density or the out-of-sample acceptance estimate of a sample split, the
leave-one-out density, or the least-squares cross-validation estimate of the integrated
squared error. The acceptance estimate is an importance-sampling average that uses the kernel
points as draws from the target, weighted by $q/\pi$; at a kernel point $q$ is the mixture
without that point's own kernel, since the importance identity requires $q$ independent of
the draw. A trial whose importance weights concentrate on a few points is rejected, and a
fit that starts among rejected trials first searches the over-smooth range for an accepted
one. The same objective can choose the kernel, by treating the Student-t degrees of
freedom $\nu$ as a second fitted parameter alongside $h$: the fit runs over
$(\ln h, \ln \nu)$ with $\nu \leq 10^4$. The kernel stays a Student-t at the upper
bound, where its log-density differs from the Gaussian kernel's by about
$[(\chi^2 - d)^2 - 2d] / (4\nu)$. The tail weight of the kernel then follows the tail
weight of the target instead of being fixed by the caller.

Center shrinkage is not fitted. The out-of-sample objective is a Kullback-Leibler criterion,
and $\mathrm{KL}(\pi \,\|\, \tilde p)$ penalizes a proposal that is too narrow far more
than one that is too wide, so it does not see the cost that a mixture wider by
$C + \kappa h^2 \langle\Sigma\rangle$ relative to $C$ imposes on the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance. Fitting it needs an
objective that penalizes both directions. Shrinkage also bounds $\nu$ from below, at
$2.5$ rather than $1$, since a kernel used with it must have a finite covariance.
